newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen calls for poll in battle for legitimacy.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen calls for poll in battle for legitimacy.

text.p: A week after battle rocked the Cambodian capital and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted his co-premier, the Cambodian strongman is facing a new type of battle -- one for legitimacy, political analysts said on Sunday.
Hun Sen's call on Sunday for a free and fair election was part of a carefully planned strategy to secure political legitimacy, and political power, the analysts said.
"I'm sure he wants to become a legitimate prime minister, that's why he has always pushed for the election," said a foreign Cambodia scholar who declined to be identified.
Hun Sen did not give a date for the poll.

He served as prime minister in the Hanoi-backed government which ruled Cambodia through the 1980s. Only a handful of countries, most of them allied to the then Soviet Union recognised that government.
Hun Sen has been second prime minister since a U.N.-organised election in 1993 and analysts said he wanted to become Cambodia's sole and legitimate prime minister.
"He cares about recognition and legitimacy," said a Cambodian political analyst. "He does not want a repeat of the isolation of the 1980s."

But while his call for a free and fair election would help him in his struggle for legitimacy, Hun Sen still had a lot to do in the aftermath of bloody battles in Phnom Penh and the ouster of First Prime Minster Prince Norodom Ranariddh, analysts said.
The violence sparked an exodus of thousands of foreigners, including many business people and aid workers.
Germany cut its aid programme and the United States suspended its aid for 30 days in response to Ranariddh's overthrow. France made no pledge of aid at a recent donor meeting in Paris.

Australia also said it was considering suspending its aid, although Sunday's Sydney-based Sun-Herald newspaper reported that Australia's ambassador in Phnom Penh had urged Canberra in a leaked diplomatic cable to back Hun Sen.

Another blow to Hun Sen was the decision of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to postpone indefinitely Cambodia's membership of the grouping, which had been scheduled for the end of this month.
"He's fighting two battles, the battle for sole power and a second battle for recognition and legitimacy," said the Cambodian analyst.
"At first he was concerned only about the battle for power. Now he has to gain legitimacy but that's not going to be so easy. Legitimacy means aid, continuing foreign assistance".
About half of Cambodia's annual budget comes from foreign aid. If that lifeline were to be cut, Hun Sen would face serious problems, including possible dissent within his own party.

"If Cambodia is back to a kind of isolation, if he's unable to prevent that, he'll have to face problems with his party," said the foreign Cambodia scholar. "That's why he's trying to deal with the international community."

"If the IMF and the World Bank come under pressure from the big countries to cut off loans," said the Cambodian source, "how is he going to pay the civil service, the police and military? How is he going to keep his own people happy?"
"It's very clear Hun Sen miscalculated the extent of the international fallout, which is monumental," a diplomat said. "There are people in his party who are not very happy with that."

The second prime minister has gone to great lengths to try to justify his action against Ranariddh and has also preserved the structure of the coalition government set up after the 1993 election. He said Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party must choose a new first prime minister, and that King Norodom Sihanouk was still head of state.
Analysts said if he is to win his battle for legitimacy he must be seen to be playing by the rules, in particular in the legislative process.
"The only source of legitimacy is the elected assembly," the foreign Cambodia scholar said.
Hun Sen will also need at least a qualified blessing from King Sihanouk. Sihanouk indicated on Sunday he would not personally endorse the new administration.
"I don't see the international community trusting a FUNCINPEC first prime minister without the support of the king," the foreign analyst said.
